postTitle: Real Returns: How to Tell if Your Portfolio Is Really Performing
topic: An account that grew €50,000 may have earned €7,000 after your own deposits and rising prices

assumptions.notes: Lesson figure: the account grew €50,000 in a year; €35,000 was added; investments earned about €15,000 (roughly 7%); inflation 4%: €8,000 only kept pace with prices; real return about €7,000.

hookVariants.narration: Your account grew fifty thousand euros this year. How much did your investments really earn?
onscreenLines: How much did your investments really earn?

beats.narration: Thirty five thousand of it was money you added yourself.
In this example, eight thousand only kept up with rising prices.
What is left, about seven thousand, is growth in what your money can buy.
This last part is the real return: growth after rising prices.

caption.instagram:
Your account grew €50,000 this year. How much did your investments really earn?

The example: €35,000 of the growth was money added during the year. The investments earned about €15,000, roughly 7%. Prices rose 4% in the same year, so about €8,000 of that only kept up with them. About €7,000 is growth in what the money can buy: a real return of about 3%.

The statement shows the first number. The others take a few minutes with the year's deposits and the inflation figure where you live.
